clue.text: Capital about a penny-a pound would be heavenly

indicators.note: the capital city goes round the next piece, so it is written about it

parts.note: Paris is the capital of France
a + d, the old abbreviation for a penny
a + l, the old abbreviation for a pound (libra)

explanation.surface: A city's finances would be blissful at a penny in the pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts AD inside PARIS to give PARADIS, then AL follows. D and L are the old pre-decimal British abbreviations for penny and pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Something paradisal is like paradise, so celestial or blissful.

clue.text: It had a dour following in French society

definitions.text: It had a dour following in French society

parts.words: It had a dour following in French society
parts.note: add the words 'a dour' after this word and you get the name of the famous mistress of Louis XV, Madame de ...

explanation.surface: A gloomy entourage at a French salon.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'a dour following' literally: put A DOUR after the answer and it becomes Pompadour, a leading figure of French court society.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomp means ceremonial splendour, the kind of display associated with the French court.

clue.text: Four ports ? Fuddled, but incorruptible

indicators.note: fuddled means confused or muddled, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Four harbours visited by a drunken sailor who still cannot be bribed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuddled' rearranges the letters of FOUR PORTS. 'incorruptible' is used in its literal sense: metal that will not corrode.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal that is rust-resistant does not decay or corrode, which is the literal sense of being incorruptible.

clue.text: Exhortation to cheerfulness from the doctor?

definitions.text: Exhortation to cheerfulness from the doctor?

parts.words: Exhortation to cheerfulness from the doctor?
parts.note: split into two words, the answer urges someone to break into song; as one word it is what a doctor does with medicine

explanation.surface: A physician telling a patient to cheer up.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as DO SING it is an exhortation to be cheerful; as one word it is the doctor giving medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Dosing is giving measured amounts of medicine, the doctor's job.

clue.text: She has different ideas

indicators.note: the letters of the word are put into a different order

explanation.surface: A woman with views unlike everyone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges IDEAS into a woman's name; 'has' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Sadie is a female first name, so it stands for a 'she'.

clue.text: The bird for a bit of sport

definitions.meaning: a prank or bit of fun

explanation.surface: Shooting a bird for sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a songbird and an escapade done for fun.

clue.text: Where Greek ships needed a blow, Iphigenia escaped one

definitions.text: Where Greek ships needed a blow, Iphigenia escaped one

parts.words: Where Greek ships needed a blow, Iphigenia escaped one
parts.note: the Greek fleet bound for Troy was becalmed at this port until Agamemnon offered his daughter Iphigenia, who in one version was whisked away by Artemis and escaped the fatal blow

explanation.surface: A tale of a becalmed fleet and a rescued princess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a blow' is first a wind for sailing, then a deathblow at the sacrifice which Iphigenia escaped.
explanation.definitionFit: Aulis is the Boeotian harbour where the Greek fleet gathered before sailing to Troy.

clue.text: Survivors or victims of forest fires?

definitions.text: Survivors or victims of forest fires?

parts.words: Survivors or victims of forest fires?
parts.note: a kind of woodland tree whose name also suggests what is left after burning

explanation.surface: Asking which trees come through a wildfire.
explanation.walkthrough: The trees are survivors of the forest, but their name sounds like what fire leaves behind: ashes.
explanation.definitionFit: These trees grow in forests, and their name recalls the residue left by burning.

clue.text: Life is proverbially of this size

definitions.text: Life is proverbially of this size

parts.words: Life is proverbially of this size
parts.note: refers to the proverb 'as ___ as life', meaning in person, unmistakably present

explanation.surface: A remark on how big life is, by the proverb.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying is 'as large as life', so the size is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'as large as life' gives life its proverbial size: big.

clue.text: It comes from the butcher rather than the baker

definitions.text: It comes from the butcher rather than the baker

parts.words: It comes from the butcher rather than the baker
parts.note: a food whose name contains 'bread' but which is offal, sold by meat traders

explanation.surface: A shopping puzzle about which shop sells an item.
explanation.walkthrough: The name ends in 'bread', pointing to the baker, but it is the pancreas or thymus of a calf or lamb, sold as meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetbread is offal, the thymus or pancreas of a young animal, so a meat trader sells it.

clue.text: He broke all the commandments

parts.note: the lawgiver who smashed the stone tablets in anger at the golden calf

explanation.surface: A sinner who broke every rule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broke' means smashed the tablets on which the Ten Commandments were written, not disobeyed them.
explanation.definitionFit: In Exodus the prophet shattered the tablets bearing the Ten Commandments.

clue.text: Presumably not to be found among light cavalry

definitions.text: Presumably not to be found among light cavalry

parts.words: Presumably not to be found among light cavalry
parts.note: a mount that is not light in colour, taken literally: an unknown contender

explanation.surface: Speculation about what a light cavalry unit would lack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'light' is read as pale in colour: a horse that is dark would not be among them. The phrase really means an unexpected contender.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark horse is a little-known competitor, read literally as a black or brown mount.

clue.text: Less effective than a stunsail ?

parts.note: read 'stunsail' as one who stuns: a smacker would be milder; both are sails

explanation.surface: Comparing two sails on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: A stunsail (studding sail) and a spanker are both sails; read as people, one who spanks is less effective than one who stuns.
explanation.definitionFit: A spanker is a fore-and-aft sail on the aftermost mast, and also one who smacks.

clue.text: "This fell sergeant, death, Is strict in his" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "This fell sergeant, death, Is strict in his" (Hamlet)

parts.words: "This fell sergeant, death, Is strict in his" (Hamlet)
parts.note: the dying Hamlet's line ends with the word for a sergeant's seizing of a prisoner

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hamlet's death scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Complete the quotation: death, like a sergeant-at-arms, is strict in his arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant's duty includes taking people into custody, and the speech ends on that word.

clue.text: They call for patient driving

parts.note: vehicles that come to collect a sick person, read as if demanding careful motoring

explanation.surface: Advice that the situation requires calm motoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'call for' means come to collect, and 'patient' is the sick person, not the adjective for careful.
explanation.definitionFit: Emergency vehicles call to pick up the sick and drive them to hospital.

clue.text: The best man embraces her

indicators.note: the words hold the name inside them, as an embrace encloses someone

explanation.surface: At a wedding, the best man hugs a guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraces' signals the run of letters inside 'tHE BEst'. Hebe, goddess of youth, was the bride of Heracles, the best of men.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebe is a goddess, so a female figure, 'her'.

clue.text: Lucy dwelt on a wild one

definitions.text: Lucy dwelt on a wild one

parts.words: Lucy dwelt on a wild one
parts.note: Wordsworth's Lucy Gray lived on a lonely heath

explanation.surface: A girl living somewhere remote.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's poem 'Lucy Gray' says she dwelt on a wide moor; 'one' stands for the open upland.
explanation.definitionFit: A moor is open uncultivated upland, the wild setting of the poem.

clue.text: Not a counter-hand in a clock-shop

definitions.text: Not a counter-hand in a clock-shop

parts.words: Not a counter-hand in a clock-shop
parts.note: someone who serves the times of the day, as if a sales assistant for clocks, but in fact an opportunist

explanation.surface: A job description: not a shop assistant at a watchmaker's.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the word is one who serves time to customers; it really means a person who trims opinions to suit the times.
explanation.definitionFit: A time-server adapts views to fashion or authority for advantage.

clue.text: Scottish hero no longer equipped for gardening

definitions.text: Scottish hero no longer equipped for gardening

indicators.note: losing a gardening tool, so the tool's name is dropped from the hero

parts.note: Ivanhoe, hero of Sir Walter Scott's novel, so Scott's hero

explanation.surface: A Highland champion who has given up his garden tools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scottish hero' is Scott's hero Ivanhoe; 'no longer equipped for gardening' takes away the HOE, leaving the first name of a Russian tsar.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan is a Russian man's name, what remains of the Scott hero after losing his tool.

clue.text: Utterly incompetent ?

parts.note: read 'utterly' as concerning uttering: unable to speak

explanation.surface: A damning verdict on someone hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utterly' means 'as regards uttering', so incompetent at speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Mute people cannot speak, so they lack competence in utterance.

clue.text: One leaves the law to the big guns

indicators.note: one letter departs from the word for a law

parts.note: an ordinance is a decree or law
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone abandons legal process for heavy weaponry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' removes I (one) from ORDINANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordnance is military artillery, the heavy guns.

clue.text: Unlike Arnold's merman

parts.note: Matthew Arnold's poem 'The Forsaken Merman' tells of one abandoned by his human wife

explanation.surface: A comparison with a poet's sea creature.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnold's poem is 'The Forsaken Merman', so unlike him means not abandoned.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not deserted is the opposite of the poem's abandoned merman.

clue.text: A princess of opera

parts.note: Verdi's Ethiopian princess, enslaved in Egypt

explanation.surface: A royal figure on the operatic stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The title heroine of Verdi's opera is an Ethiopian princess.

clue.text: The last to keep sober ?

parts.note: an ordinal place in a series, read with 'sober' hinting that eight drinks leaves a person drunk

explanation.surface: Who will stay sober longest at a party?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the last person sober; it points to a position in a line, perhaps last of a rowing eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighth is an ordinal, the final place in a group of eight.

clue.text: "Unarm, Eros", he cried

parts.note: the Roman general in Shakespeare's tragedy speaks this line to his servant Eros

explanation.surface: Someone tells the god of love to drop his weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: Eros here is not the god but a servant in 'Antony and Cleopatra', whom the general asks to remove his armour.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare gives this line to Mark Antony, addressing his attendant Eros.

clue.text: Portion of bird is a pound in weight

indicators.note: the pound sits inside the weight

parts.note: a ton is a unit of weight
a + l, the abbreviation for pound (libra)

explanation.surface: A butcher weighing out a share of poultry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Portion of bird' suggests a cut of poultry, but it is the claw; L for pound comes from the Latin libra.
explanation.definitionFit: A talon is the claw of a bird of prey, part of the creature.

clue.text: Demanded decimal conversion

indicators.note: converting changes form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone insisted on switching to decimal currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conversion' rearranges DECIMAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To have claimed something is to have asserted a right to it.

clue.text: Not the best man

parts.note: read as wedding role, but meaning the one who came off worse in a contest

explanation.surface: A remark about who stands beside the groom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'best man' suggests a wedding; here it is just the man who did not win.
explanation.definitionFit: A loser is the one defeated, not the winner.

clue.text: Inclination of painter and legislator

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: The leanings of an artist and a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of London's Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramp is a slope, so an incline.

clue.text: He makes sure of his change

indicators.note: the letters are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: A careful man checking his coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges SURE; 'makes' and 'of his' link.
explanation.definitionFit: A user is a person who uses something, so a 'he'.

clue.text: They just mark time

parts.note: read as idling, but meaning objects that record the days and months

explanation.surface: Complaint about people who make no progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mark time' usually means to stall; here it is literal: these record the passing of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Calendars set out days, weeks and months, so they record time.

clue.text: The flighty take to them

parts.note: the idiom 'take to one's ...' means to run away, so those prone to flight

explanation.surface: Fickle people are drawn to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flighty' is read as given to flight, fleeing; they 'take to their heels'.
explanation.definitionFit: To take to one's heels is to run off, so fugitives use these.

clue.text: His riders took to the sea

definitions.text: His riders took to the sea

parts.words: His riders took to the sea
parts.note: the Irish playwright wrote the one-act tragedy 'Riders to the Sea'

explanation.surface: A tale of horsemen heading into the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: The riders are from the title of the play 'Riders to the Sea' by J. M. Synge.
explanation.definitionFit: John Millington Synge, Irish dramatist, wrote 'Riders to the Sea'.

clue.text: Presumably a song is not dear to him

definitions.text: Presumably a song is not dear to him

parts.words: Presumably a song is not dear to him
parts.note: 'for a song' means very cheap, so the buyer finds it inexpensive rather than beloved

explanation.surface: Someone who doesn't care for a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dear' means expensive, not beloved; things bought 'for a song' are cheap to the buyer.
explanation.definitionFit: A purchaser is a buyer, the one who pays the price.
